chapter: The craft of the ad lib player
title: Self-criticism, out-of-tune pianos and difficulty of instruments
summary: Musicians as harsh judges of themselves, anecdotes of bad pianos and which instruments are hardest.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well, you often think musicians are harder on themselves than anyone else because --

-- I mean as a professional listener myself who doesn't always listen as a critic, can, you know, listen for enjoyment. I'll go up to a musician and say, you know, sincerely you really played beautifully tonight, and they'll say, no, I wasn't really getting it, you know, and I can, you know, not up to my own expectations.

Right. Well, not only that, you hear things that the listener isn't even aware of, maybe the tempo, length of the note or the sound of the note or anything, you know, that you're well aware of. All of you -- well, like I said, your instrument is an extension of yourself. So what it means is that you've got this impersonal instrument that you have got to make say something, and you're listening to yourself, not amplified, but another appendage-like. I don't know if I'm explaining that to you.

Well, I understand it. And the pianist has the hardest job in a way because sometimes the instruments he's given to work on or work with are inferior; whereas usually the other instruments are -- the personal property of the musicians, and they care for them in such a way that, you know, they usually perform, although there are always technical breakdowns with your, you know, with your own instruments, because they're only manmade tools.
Well, I don't -- I don't give piano a priority on being that difficult because it's a fixed instrument.

Yeah, but I mean you go into some clubs, and the pianos have been terrible, whereas you bring your bass to work, and, you know, sometimes you might have some problems with it that you hadn't been able to have repaired, but generally speaking, you know, it is in working order, and
Right, yes. I remember working on an engagement with Teddy Wilson, and the piano was so badly out of tune that he played in one key, and we played in another.

Well, that's something. We won't get into that. But I -- you know, I've been in situations where I've had to pull the mouthpiece on a saxophone out so far, put a piece of shirt cardboard on the end to get it, you know, because you couldn't possibly get in tuned --

But I think the instruments that have to be fingered are much more difficult than the piano as a fixed instrument. Trombonist, for instance, the slide and the positions and dexterity, you know; stringed instruments.
